newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-VW predicts 1997 profits to outpace sales.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-VW predicts 1997 profits to outpace sales.

text.p: German carmaker Volkswagen AG said on Thursday it expected 1997 profits to outpace sales growth after results last year received a hefty lift from the German mark's decline in foreign exchange markets.

VW said in its 1996 annual report issued on Thursday that it expected "postive results" for 1997 despite forecasts for slow consumer spending as many European nations slash spending to qualify for European currency union set to begin in 1999.
"We expect our 1997 earnings to outpace sales growth," VW chief financial officer Bruno Adelt said in the text of a speech at the carmaker's annual news conference.

The German carmaker's forecast comes after it earlier this year reported a near doubling in 1996 group profit to 678 million marks ($393.5 million) from 336 million marks behind a 10.6 percent growth in sales to 3.977 billion marks and a 10 percent growth in group vehicle sales to nearly four million units.

VW said its 1996 results were aided by about 600 million marks in gains from foreign currency market turbulence and the weakening of the mark against the dollar, lira and pound in late 1996 that reduced the cost of vehicles sold abroad.
VW chief executive Ferdinand Piech sounded a cautious note, saying that "a continuation of the current economic conditions would lead us to expect positive developments for the year".

VW, considered Europe's largest carmaker, said in the annual report that it expected the German economy to be aided by exports in 1997 but to overall show limited growth and little improvement in the jobless crisis that may curb sales.
But slower sales growth in Germany and western Europe should be compensated for by higher growth rates in Asia and Latin America as VW steps up its international expansion.

"In consideration of these factors, the vehicle industry can expect a small increase in global vehicle demand. We expect positive impulses from markets in Asia, Latin America, as well as in Middle and Eastern Europe," VW said in the report.
But the carmaker noted, "For western Europe and Germany, we are expecting a small increase in demand."
VW's first-quarter sales reflected the forecast with a 9.5 percent increase in customer deliveries amid double-digit growth in foreign markets but slow growth in western Europe.
Piech said VW saw an increase of 27.9 percent in eastern Europe and a 15.2 percent gain in North America.
But customer deliveries in western Europe, which is the carmaker's largest market, rose a mere 2.5 percent, VW said.
In other regions, VW said Latin America and Africa sales rose 17.9 percent and Asia-Pacific sales were up 26.5 percent.
VW also said it has seen strong demand for its new Passat saloon and would increase 1997 production by up to 25 percent.
Piech told journalists late on Wednesday that VW may boost Passat output by up to 100,000 units from the planned 300,000, in part due to demand for a new estate wagon version.

The strong demand for the Passat, at the top end of the VW brand product range, comes as VW said on Thursday it would expand its product line to about 50 models in the next three years from the current level of 38 models.
"The expansion of our product line is going to accelerate in the coming years," Piech said in the text of a speech at the carmaker's annual news conference scheduled for Thursday.

Piech defended VW's future goal of using only four vehicle platform basic structures to build cars under the VW, Skoda, Seat and Audi brands, dismissing criticism by some industry observers that there was not enough differentiation between the brands.
Some industry observers have said cars so far produced on common platforms have been too similar and may "cannibalise" sales within the VW group, a view generally rejected by Piech.

"We remain convinced that the platform strategy that we have developed is still the best way for us to remain competitive," Piech said, noting the carmaker currently uses 19 different platforms within the group.

Piech, however, did concede that the introduction of the new Passat had reduced demand last year for the Audi A4 model more than the carmaker had expected but still led to 16 growth in demand for the two vehicles combined over 1995 levels.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.722 German Marks)
